title: The Book on Trial: Galileo before the Holy Office
subtitle: The trial of Galileo Galilei and the Dialogue, Rome, Florence and Siena, 1632–1634 (with the 1616 injunction and the 1992 papal address)
intro: In February 1632 a Florentine press finished printing Galileo's Dialogue on the Two Chief World Systems, a conversation in Italian among three friends weighing Ptolemy against Copernicus. It carried the licence of the Master of the Sacred Palace in Rome and the Florentine inquisitor. By late summer it was impounded. In September Pope Urban VIII, who as Cardinal Maffeo Barberini had been Galileo's admirer, sent the case to the Congregation of the Holy Office. Ten months later, on 22 June 1633, Galileo knelt in the Dominican convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, heard himself declared 'vehemently suspect of heresy', and abjured.

This is a trial built from letters and from the court's own file, not from diaries. The Holy Office kept minutes, depositions taken down by a notary in Latin and Italian, consultors' reports, a papal decision and the sentence; the file stayed in the Vatican and was published in full only in the nineteenth century, with modern critical editions since. Beside it run the dispatches of Francesco Niccolini, the Tuscan ambassador who housed Galileo, which are the main source for what Urban VIII said in private audiences. The Pope's words reach us only through Niccolini's reports, and the form tags say so. Galileo's own letters, and the weekly letters of his daughter Suor Maria Celeste from her convent at Arcetri, give the view from the accused's family. Most of these texts are in Italian and appear here as paraphrase, drawn from Antonio Favaro's Edizione Nazionale (1890–1909); short quotations come only from English translations published before 1929.

The legal heart of the case was a single sheet. In the 1616 file was an unsigned minute stating that on 26 February 1616 the Commissary of the Holy Office, in Cardinal Bellarmine's presence, had ordered Galileo not to hold, teach or defend Copernicus's opinion 'in any way whatever'. Galileo held a certificate from Bellarmine, dated 26 May 1616, saying only that he had been told of the general decree. Whether that minute records what was actually said, and why it is unsigned, has been argued over since it came to light. Historians remain divided, and the chapter sets the documents side by side rather than deciding.

Around the court stand the people who wrote while the case went on: the Commissary Vincenzo Maculano, who talked Galileo into a plea in a private session and reported it to the Cardinal-nephew Francesco Barberini; Benedetto Castelli, Galileo's former pupil; Archbishop Ascanio Piccolomini of Siena, who took the condemned man into his palace; the Servite Fulgenzio Micanzio in Venice; and, abroad, Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc in Provence and René Descartes in the Netherlands, who hid his own treatise on the world when the news reached him. Behind them the plague of 1630–33 shut roads, put Galileo in quarantine on the Tuscan border and filled Maria Celeste's letters with remedies and deaths.

Two famous elements are absent or flagged. The words 'Eppur si muove' ('and yet it moves'), supposedly muttered after the abjuration, appear in no record of 1633. They first appear in print in Giuseppe Baretti's Italian Library (London, 1757), and on a Spanish painting of Galileo in prison whose date and attribution are uncertain; they are a legend. The chapter ends with the dated facts of afterward: Galileo confined at Arcetri, Peiresc's plea of December 1634, and Pope John Paul II's address of 31 October 1992 to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences. That address was widely reported as a rehabilitation but was not a formal annulment of the 1633 sentence.
calendar_note: Rome, Florence and Siena used the Gregorian calendar from 1582, so all dates are New Style and need no conversion. One trap remains in the letters: Florence counted the year from 25 March (stile fiorentino) until 1750, so a Florentine letter of March 1633 may be dated '1632' in the original. Favaro's edition normalises these, and the dates here follow modern style. Descartes and Peiresc in France and the Dutch Republic also wrote in New Style. Some English versions print Galileo's letter to Diodati of 25 July 1634 as 24 July; Favaro's text gives the 25th.

eyes.name: Galileo Galilei
eyes.role: Philosopher and Chief Mathematician to the Grand Duke of Tuscany, aged 68–70; author of the Dialogue (1632)
eyes.side: the accused; Medici court of Tuscany
eyes.where: Florence and his villa at Arcetri; Rome (Tuscan embassy at Villa Medici and the Holy Office palace), February–July 1633; Siena, July–December 1633; Arcetri from December 1633

waypoints.label: Plague quarantine at Ponte a Centino, Jan–Feb 1633
Rome, Tuscan embassy at Villa Medici, Feb 1633
Holy Office palace, April and June 1633

eyes.form: depositions (court record), written defence, abjuration and dated letters
eyes.authenticity: His four depositions, defence and abjuration survive in the Holy Office file (Vatican Secret Archives), recorded by the court notary; letters survive in autograph or copy and are edited in Favaro's Edizione Nazionale, vols. XIV–XVI. The depositions are the court's record of his answers, not his own drafting, except the written defence of 10 May 1633, which he composed.
eyes.bio: Galileo had made his name in 1610 with the telescope and the moons of Jupiter, and in 1632 published the Dialogue believing he had papal leave to discuss Copernicus as a hypothesis. He arrived in Rome ill and nearly seventy, and his letters swing from confidence that his innocence would be recognised to pleas for release. He is the only eye who speaks both inside the court record and outside it.

sources.title: Le Opere di Galileo Galilei, Edizione Nazionale (Favaro), vol. XV, Carteggio 1633 (Liber Liber text)
Galileo, Lettere (Liber Liber selection, incl. letters to Cioli, F. Barberini, Bocchineri and Diodati 1632–34)
Famous Trials: The Trial of Galileo (depositions, defence, sentence, abjuration in English)

eyes.name: Congregation of the Holy Office (Roman Inquisition) — the trial file
eyes.role: The tribunal of ten cardinal-inquisitors, with the Pope as prefect, its Commissary, Assessor, notary and consultors
eyes.where: Rome: the Holy Office palace beside St Peter's; the sentence read at Santa Maria sopra Minerva
eyes.form: court record (minutes, injunction, consultors' reports, decree, sentence, circulars)
eyes.authenticity: The file of the Galileo proceedings is preserved in the Vatican Secret (now Apostolic) Archives; it was taken to Paris under Napoleon and returned in 1846, and published by Domenico Berti, Karl von Gebler and Henri de L'Épinois in the 1870s, then by Favaro (vol. XIX). The 26 February 1616 injunction is an unsigned minute, and its status is disputed among historians.
eyes.bio: The Holy Office was the Roman congregation for heresy, created in 1542 as part of the Catholic response to the Reformation. Its record is terse and procedural, and it is the only voice here that never explains itself. Its documents fix the legal case: a 1616 order, a book judged to defend that order's forbidden opinion, and a defendant who could be 'vehemently suspected'.

sources.title: Finocchiaro, The Galileo Affair: A Documentary History (1989) — document list with dates (course handout)
Popular Science Monthly 67 (June 1905), 'Galileo IV' (English summary and translation of the trial record)

eyes.name: Cardinal Robert Bellarmine SJ
eyes.role: Jesuit cardinal and senior member of the Holy Office in 1616; dead by the time of the trial
eyes.where: Rome, his residence near the Roman College
eyes.authenticity: The original certificate of 26 May 1616, in Bellarmine's hand, was kept by Galileo and produced at his third deposition in 1633; a copy is in the trial file. Edited in Favaro, vol. XIX.
eyes.bio: Bellarmine, the leading Catholic controversialist of his age, had written in 1615 that Copernicanism could be held only hypothetically unless proved. In 1616 he delivered the Holy Office's warning to Galileo. His certificate became Galileo's main defence in 1633, because its wording did not match the unsigned injunction in the file.

sources.title: Finocchiaro document list: Bellarmine's certificate, 26 May 1616

eyes.name: Pope Urban VIII (Maffeo Barberini)
eyes.role: Pope from 1623, aged 64–65; prefect of the Holy Office; once Galileo's patron
eyes.where: Rome, the papal palace (Quirinal) and Castel Gandolfo
eyes.vantage_label: the judge above the judges (heard through the ambassador)
eyes.form: reported speech in diplomatic dispatches; papal decree in the court record
eyes.authenticity: No diary or letter of Urban VIII on the case is used here. His words come from Niccolini's dispatches to Florence, written the same day or the next and reflecting the ambassador's memory and purposes; his formal decision of 16 June 1633 is in the Holy Office minutes.
eyes.bio: As cardinal, Maffeo Barberini wrote a Latin poem in Galileo's praise and in 1624 received him six times in audience. The Dialogue put the Pope's own favourite argument, that God could produce any effect in ways beyond human knowing, into the mouth of the character Simplicio near its end, and Urban came to believe he had been deceived over the licence. In 1632 he was also under attack from the Spanish cardinals over his politics in the Thirty Years' War.

sources.title: Favaro, vol. XIV (Niccolini's dispatches of September 1632)
Popular Science Monthly 67 (June 1905), 'Galileo IV'

eyes.name: Francesco Niccolini
eyes.role: Tuscan ambassador in Rome (1621–1643), aged 48–49; Galileo's host and advocate
eyes.where: Rome, the Tuscan embassy at Villa Medici on the Pincio (Trinità dei Monti)
eyes.vantage_label: the ambassador in the papal audience room
eyes.authenticity: Original dispatches to the Secretary of State Andrea Cioli survive in the Archivio di Stato, Florence (Mediceo del Principato); edited in Favaro, vols. XIV–XV. They are official reports written to influence policy in Florence, and they also served as the conduit for the Pope's words.
eyes.bio: Niccolini had met Galileo in 1624 and helped steer the Dialogue past the Roman licenser. For five months he and his wife, Caterina Riccardi Niccolini, a cousin of the licenser, kept Galileo in their house, and he told Florence he would pay the costs himself if need be. His dispatches are the nearest thing to a diary of the trial from outside the courtroom.

sources.title: Favaro, vol. XV (dispatches of 1633)
Museo Galileo, biography of Francesco Niccolini

eyes.name: Vincenzo Maculano da Firenzuola OP
eyes.role: Dominican friar, Commissary General of the Holy Office, the trial's examining judge; also a military engineer
eyes.form: official letter; the depositions taken before him
eyes.authenticity: His letter of 28 April 1633 to Cardinal Francesco Barberini survives in the Barberini papers (Vatican Library) and was published by Favaro; it is the only inside account of the plea arrangement.
eyes.bio: Maculano conducted the depositions. After the first hearing he obtained leave to speak with Galileo outside the formal procedure and persuaded him to admit fault, so the court could close the case with lenience. He later became a cardinal and built fortifications for the papacy.

sources.title: Finocchiaro document list: Firenzuola to Cardinal Barberini, 28 April 1633
Popular Science Monthly 67 (June 1905), 'Galileo IV' (English version of the letter)

eyes.name: Cardinal Francesco Barberini
eyes.role: Cardinal-nephew of Urban VIII, aged 35–37; a cardinal-inquisitor of the Holy Office
eyes.vantage_label: the Pope's nephew on the tribunal
eyes.authenticity: His letters survive in the Barberini archive and are edited in Favaro, vols. XIV–XVI. His name is among the three of the ten cardinals that do not appear on the surviving sentence; the reason is not recorded.
eyes.bio: Francesco Barberini handled much of the Holy Office's correspondence on the case, received Maculano's report and was the channel to whom Galileo, Niccolini and later Peiresc wrote for mercy. He was a patron of learning, and his absence from the sentence's signatures has been read both as quiet sympathy and as mere absence. The record does not settle it.

sources.title: Favaro, vol. XIV (letter of 25 September 1632)
Favaro, vol. XVI (reply to Peiresc, 2 January 1635)

eyes.name: Suor Maria Celeste (Virginia Galilei)
eyes.role: Galileo's elder daughter, aged 32–33; Poor Clare nun at the convent of San Matteo, Arcetri
eyes.side: the accused's family; the enclosed convent
eyes.where: Convent of San Matteo in Arcetri, near Galileo's villa, outside Florence
eyes.vantage_label: the daughter at home, waiting for letters
eyes.authenticity: 124 autograph letters (1623–1633) were found among Galileo's papers and are in the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Florence; edited in Favaro and translated by Dava Sobel (2001). Galileo's replies are lost. She wrote knowing letters to Rome might be read by others.
eyes.bio: Placed in the convent at thirteen, Maria Celeste ran her father's household from behind the grille: wine, the mule, the garden, the debts. Her weekly letters of 1633 set plague deaths and convent illness beside her fears for him, and after the sentence she quietly took over his penance. She died on 2 April 1634, four months after his return.

sources.title: Favaro, vol. XV (her letters of 1633)
Sobel (trans.), Letters to Father (Wellcome Collection catalogue record)

eyes.name: Benedetto Castelli OSB
eyes.role: Benedictine monk, mathematician at the Sapienza in Rome; Galileo's former pupil, aged 54–55
eyes.vantage_label: friend in Rome, then sent away
eyes.authenticity: Autograph letters to Galileo in the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Florence; edited in Favaro, vols. XIV–XVI.
eyes.bio: It was Galileo's 1613 letter to Castelli on Scripture and astronomy that first brought Galileo to the Holy Office's attention in 1615. In 1632 Castelli read the Dialogue with delight; during the trial he was absent in Brescia, writing to Galileo about pensions and providence.

sources.title: Favaro, vol. XIV (letters of 1632)
Favaro, vol. XV (letters of 1633)

eyes.name: Ascanio II Piccolomini
eyes.role: Archbishop of Siena from 1628, aged 42–44; a friend and admirer of Galileo
eyes.authenticity: Letters to Galileo edited in Favaro, vols. XV–XVI. An anonymous denunciation of his hospitality to the Holy Office, said to date from 1634, is not used here.
eyes.bio: Piccolomini wrote to Galileo throughout the trial, offering litters, servants and a refuge. From July to December 1633 Galileo lived in his palace, where he went back to work on the science of motion that became the Two New Sciences (1638).

sources.title: Favaro, vol. XV
Favaro, vol. XVI (letter of 11 April 1634)

eyes.name: Fra Fulgenzio Micanzio OSM
eyes.role: Servite friar, theologian to the Venetian Republic, disciple and biographer of Paolo Sarpi
eyes.side: Venice, a state that had defied papal interdict in 1606
eyes.vantage_label: a friend in the republic beyond Rome's reach
eyes.authenticity: Letters to Galileo edited in Favaro, vol. XVI.
eyes.bio: Micanzio wrote to Galileo frequently from 1634, urging him to keep working and to publish. His letters are the freest in tone in the whole correspondence, because they came from Venice, where the Inquisition's reach was limited by the Republic.

sources.title: Favaro, vol. XVI (Carteggio 1634–1636)

eyes.name: Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc
eyes.role: Provençal antiquary, astronomer and councillor in the Parlement of Aix, aged 53–54; a correspondent of Cardinal Francesco Barberini
eyes.authenticity: Peiresc's letters to the Dupuy brothers, Gassendi and Barberini are preserved in Carpentras and Paris and partly edited in Favaro, vols. XV–XVI.
eyes.bio: Peiresc followed the case from Provence, passing the printed sentence to Gassendi and trading rumours with the Dupuys in Paris. In December 1634 he used his friendship with Cardinal Barberini to plead directly for Galileo, the boldest intervention any Catholic outsider made.

sources.title: Favaro, vol. XVI (Peiresc to F. Barberini, 5 December 1634)

eyes.name: René Descartes
eyes.role: French philosopher living in the Dutch Republic, aged 37; finishing a treatise, Le Monde
eyes.authenticity: Letters to Marin Mersenne, published by Clerselier (1657–67) and in Adam & Tannery; dates supplied by editors in brackets. Reprinted in Favaro, vols. XV–XVI.
eyes.bio: Descartes had nearly finished a physics of the whole world built on the Earth's motion when he learned that Galileo had been condemned. He chose not to publish, and Le Monde appeared only after his death. He is the clearest case of the trial's effect on people who were never in Rome.

sources.title: Favaro, vol. XV (Descartes to Mersenne, end of November 1633)

eyes.name: Pope John Paul II (Karol Wojtyła)
eyes.where: Vatican, Sala Regia, plenary session of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences
eyes.vantage_label: the epilogue, three and a half centuries on
eyes.language: French (delivered); published in Italian and English by the Holy See
eyes.authenticity: Official text published by the Holy See (vatican.va) and in Acta Apostolicae Sedis; accompanied by Cardinal Paul Poupard's report on the work of the study commission.
eyes.bio: In November 1979 John Paul II asked theologians, scientists and historians to re-examine the case, and a commission worked through the 1980s. His 1992 address accepted that Galileo's judges had erred, while presenting the episode as a tragic failure of understanding on both sides. It did not annul the sentence, and historians have argued over how far it went.

sources.title: Address to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, 31 October 1992 (vatican.va, Italian PDF)

entries.headline: An unsigned minute: never to hold, teach or defend
entries.digest: A minute in the Holy Office file records that Bellarmine warned Galileo that the Copernican opinion was to be abandoned. It adds that the Commissary, Michelangelo Seghizzi, then ordered him not to hold, teach or defend it in any way, orally or in writing, on pain of prison. The minute carries no signature of Galileo or of a notary. Its witnesses appear to be members of Bellarmine's household. This sheet, found in 1632, became the legal basis of the charge of disobedience.
entries.source_note: Holy Office file, 'Special Injunction' 26 Feb 1616 (Finocchiaro, The Galileo Affair, pp. 147–48); status disputed

entries.headline: Bellarmine certifies: no abjuration, no penance
entries.digest: To answer rumours in Florence and Pisa that he had abjured and been punished, Galileo asked Bellarmine for a written statement. The cardinal certified that Galileo had abjured nothing and received no penance. He had only been told of the declaration that the Earth's motion could not be defended or held. The certificate says nothing about 'teaching' or 'in any way whatever'. Galileo kept the original and produced it seventeen years later.
entries.source_note: Bellarmine's certificate, 26 May 1616 (Finocchiaro p. 153); produced at the 10 May 1633 hearing

entries.headline: The Dialogue comes off the press
entries.digest: Giovanni Battista Landini in Florence finished printing the Dialogue on the Two Chief World Systems, and Galileo presented the first copy to Grand Duke Ferdinando II the next day. It bore Roman and Florentine imprimaturs, a preface stating that the Copernican view was treated hypothetically, and a closing argument from divine omnipotence spoken by the Aristotelian Simplicio. Plague quarantines slowed copies reaching Rome until the spring.
entries.source_note: Standard chronology (Finocchiaro; Museo Galileo); Niccolini to Cioli 28 March 1632 on books held in lazarettos (Favaro XIV no. 2254)

entries.headline: Castelli reads it again and again
entries.digest: Castelli told Galileo the book was very beautiful and that he had read it through repeatedly. He enjoyed the beating Simplicio took and laughed at the critics. He advised his old teacher to ignore his opponents. Three weeks later he added that the Jesuit astronomer Christoph Scheiner had been visibly agitated on hearing the book praised.
entries.source_note: Castelli to Galileo, Rome 29 May 1632 (Favaro XIV no. 2275); 19 June 1632 (no. 2277)

entries.place: Rome, papal audience (reported in Niccolini's dispatch of 5 September)
entries.headline: The Pope erupts: Galileo has meddled
entries.digest: When Niccolini came to plead for the book, the Pope burst out in anger. He said that Galileo had entered on the gravest and most dangerous subjects, and that the licence had been obtained by a trick. He named his own former secretary Giovanni Ciampoli and the licenser as having let him down. He told the ambassador that the Grand Duke should not involve himself. Niccolini's covering advice the next day was to make no protest and work quietly through ministers and Cardinal Francesco Barberini.
entries.quote: ventured to meddle with things that he ought not
entries.source_note: Niccolini to Cioli, Rome 5 Sept 1632 (Favaro XIV no. 2298); English in Popular Science Monthly 67 (1905), 'Galileo IV'

entries.headline: A warning from the files of 1616
entries.digest: Niccolini passed on what the licenser, the Dominican Niccolò Riccardi, had told him: the Pope regarded the book as touching faith and Scripture. Riccardi had also mentioned an old order in the Holy Office files forbidding Galileo to treat the subject. This was the first hint in Florence of the injunction minute. Niccolini urged that Tuscany make no protests and let Galileo quietly revise the book.
entries.source_note: Niccolini to Cioli, Rome 11 Sept 1632 (Favaro XIV no. 2302)

entries.place: Rome, papal audience that morning (reported by Niccolini)
entries.headline: The Pope sends the case to the Inquisition
entries.digest: In a second audience the Pope told Niccolini that a special commission had gone over the book and was sending it to the Holy Office. He refused to let Galileo's side know the charges in advance and swore the ambassador to secrecy under pain of censure. He warned that Galileo's opinions could spread to his students. He still spoke of Galileo as a friend whom he had treated well.
entries.source_note: Niccolini to Cioli, Rome 18 Sept 1632 (Favaro XIV no. 2305); cf. Popular Science Monthly 67 (1905)

entries.place: Rome, Congregation of the Holy Office, the Pope presiding
entries.headline: Summon Galileo to Rome in October
entries.digest: With the special commission's report before it, the Congregation ordered the Florentine inquisitor to summon Galileo to Rome during October. He was to be notified before a notary and witnesses, so that he could not later claim he had not been told. The order was carried out on 1 October, when Galileo signed an acknowledgement and promised to obey.
entries.source_note: Holy Office minutes, 23 Sept 1632 (Popular Science Monthly 67, 1905; Finocchiaro); Galileo's acknowledgement 1 Oct 1632

entries.headline: The nephew sends the summons north
entries.digest: Cardinal Francesco Barberini wrote to the papal nuncio in Florence, Giorgio Bolognetti, instructing that the inquisitor summon Galileo to Rome within the month. A second letter of the same day set out what to do if Galileo refused. The courtesy of the Pope's own nephew handling the matter did not soften its terms.
entries.source_note: F. Barberini to Bolognetti, Rome 25 Sept 1632 (Favaro XIV nos. 2311–2312)

entries.headline: Galileo begs to be tried by letter
entries.digest: Galileo wrote to Cardinal Francesco Barberini that he had expected critics but not a ban on circulation. He said he believed rivals were behind it. Citing his age of nearly seventy, his chronic illnesses and the plague on the roads, he asked to submit a written defence or be heard in Florence. He promised to come to Rome if no other way was allowed.
entries.source_note: Galileo to F. Barberini, Florence 13 Oct 1632 (Favaro XIV no. 2324; Lettere XVII)

entries.headline: Castelli vouches for his teacher's innocence
entries.digest: Castelli assured Galileo that he was innocent and that the best people in Rome were speaking well of him. He offered to do anything he could in the city. The letter is a friend's encouragement at a moment when Galileo was under orders to travel or be fetched.
entries.source_note: Castelli to Galileo, Rome 7 Jan 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2379)

entries.headline: The doctors' certificate has gone badly
entries.digest: Niccolini reported to Cioli that the medical certificate had been badly received in Rome and was being taken as a delaying trick. The best course was for Galileo to set out at once. Five days later, on 20 January, Galileo left Florence for Rome.
entries.source_note: Niccolini to Cioli, Rome 15 Jan 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2387)

entries.headline: To Diodati, on the eve of the journey
entries.digest: On the same day Galileo wrote at length to his Paris friend Elia Diodati about how the Dialogue was being received by Diodati and Gassendi. He defended the view that Scripture is not meant to settle questions of nature.
entries.source_note: Galileo to Diodati, Florence 15 Jan 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2384)

entries.headline: Keep cheerful, father
entries.digest: While Galileo sat out his plague quarantine at the Tuscan border, his daughter sent convent news to Rome. Suor Luisa, her closest companion, was ill. She begged him to keep his spirits up. The letter is the first of the weekly series she kept up through the whole trial.
entries.source_note: Maria Celeste to Galileo, Arcetri 5 Feb 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2404)

entries.headline: Galileo is here
entries.digest: Niccolini reported that Galileo had reached Rome, by the standard chronology on the evening of 13 February after twenty-odd days in quarantine. He was lodged in the embassy and the ambassador was already at work with officials. Two days later he wrote that Galileo was keeping indoors, on a cardinal's advice, while the case was pending.
entries.source_note: Niccolini to Cioli, Rome 14 and 16 Feb 1633 (Favaro XV nos. 2408–2409)

entries.headline: The crux is the order of 1616
entries.digest: In audience the Pope told Niccolini that Galileo had been badly advised to publish his opinions. Niccolini wrote that the main difficulty was the charge that Galileo had been forbidden in 1616 to discuss the Copernican opinion at all. The other points, he thought, would be easier to get over.
entries.source_note: Niccolini to Cioli, Rome 27 Feb 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2428); Popular Science Monthly 67 (1905)

entries.headline: The archbishop hopes for a just end
entries.digest: Two days before the first hearing, Archbishop Piccolomini wrote from Siena that he hoped the case would end with Galileo's sincerity and innocence recognised. He asked to hear from him. Through the spring he kept repeating his invitation to Siena once the case was settled.
entries.source_note: Piccolomini to Galileo, Siena 10 April 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2462); 16 and 28 May 1633 (nos. 2510, 2525)

entries.headline: First deposition: he does not remember 'in any way'
entries.digest: Before Maculano, Galileo acknowledged the Dialogue as his and described the 1616 meetings. Bellarmine, he said, had told him the opinion could not be held or defended. He produced the certificate and said he did not remember any order not to teach it 'in any way whatever'. He maintained the book did not hold or defend Copernicus but showed his arguments to be inconclusive. He had not told the licenser of the 1616 order because he did not think it applied. He was then kept at the Holy Office.
entries.source_note: First deposition, 12 April 1633 (Finocchiaro pp. 256–62; Popular Science Monthly 67, 1905)

entries.place: Rome, rooms of the Holy Office Fiscal
entries.headline: Detained, but in the prosecutor's own rooms
entries.digest: Galileo told Geri Bocchineri in Florence that he was being held not in a cell but in the apartment of the Fiscal, the Holy Office prosecutor. He described the arrangement as an unusual courtesy, with comforts not normally given to those under examination.
entries.source_note: Galileo to Bocchineri, Rome 16 April 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2466)

entries.headline: Examined, held, and no date for release
entries.digest: Niccolini confirmed to Cioli that Galileo had been examined on the 12th and was lodged in the Fiscal's rooms. No one would say when he might be released.
entries.source_note: Niccolini to Cioli, Rome 16 April 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2471)

entries.headline: Three consultors: the book defends Copernicus
entries.digest: Three theologians appointed by the Holy Office filed opinions on the Dialogue: Agostino Oreggi, the Jesuit Melchior Inchofer and the Theatine Zaccaria Pasqualigo. All three concluded that the book taught or defended the Earth's motion, contrary to the 1616 order. Inchofer, the most severe, argued that Galileo held the opinion, not merely discussed it. Their reports undercut the defence Galileo had just offered.
entries.source_note: Consultants' reports, 17 April 1633 (Finocchiaro p. 276)

entries.headline: News that he is shut in
entries.digest: Maria Celeste had heard that her father was confined at the Holy Office. She urged him to stay calm and put his trust in God. Three days later she begged him not to try to travel home while plague was still killing in Florence.
entries.source_note: Maria Celeste to Galileo, Arcetri 20 and 23 April 1633 (Favaro XV nos. 2474, 2480)

entries.headline: Writing from bed, in pain
entries.digest: Galileo wrote briefly to Bocchineri that he had been in bed for sixteen hours with violent pain in his thigh. Officials of the Holy Office had visited him and promised to finish the case once he recovered. He trusted this promise more than earlier ones. He still expected his innocence to be acknowledged and sent greetings to the family and the nuns.
entries.source_note: Galileo to Bocchineri, Rome 23 April 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2478; Lettere XX)

entries.headline: The Commissary arranges a plea
entries.digest: Maculano reported to Cardinal Francesco Barberini that the cardinals had authorised him the day before to treat with Galileo out of court. After long argument Galileo had admitted that he had gone too far in the book and agreed to confess it formally. This would let the tribunal show leniency and save its reputation, and the case could be closed quickly. He noted Galileo's poor health and proposed sending him back to the embassy.
entries.quote: I brought him into a full sense of his error
entries.source_note: Maculano (Firenzuola) to F. Barberini, 28 April 1633 (Finocchiaro pp. 276–77); English in Popular Science Monthly 67 (1905)

entries.headline: Second deposition: 'vainglorious ambition'
entries.digest: As arranged, Galileo said he had reread the Dialogue after three years and found that parts of it, against his intention, made the Copernican arguments look stronger than he believed them. He blamed vanity and the pleasure of seeming clever, not a wish to defy the Church. He then offered to add a day or two to the dialogue refuting those arguments. That same day he was sent back to the embassy.
entries.quote: one of vainglorious ambition, and of pure ignorance and inadvertence
entries.source_note: Second deposition, 30 April 1633 (Finocchiaro pp. 277–79); English in Popular Science Monthly 67 (1905)

entries.headline: Sent home early, thanks to the Commissary
entries.digest: Niccolini reported that Galileo had been released to the embassy before the case was complete, through the Commissary's intercession with Cardinal Barberini. Two days later he wrote that Galileo seemed in better health and that the Commissary might come to close the case.
entries.source_note: Niccolini to Cioli, Rome 1 and 3 May 1633 (Favaro XV nos. 2490, 2493)

entries.headline: Joy, and a recipe against plague
entries.digest: Hearing that he was back at the embassy, Maria Celeste wrote that she was overjoyed. She enclosed a remedy against the plague. Through May her letters mix garden news and household accounts with warnings not to come home while the contagion lasted.
entries.source_note: Maria Celeste to Galileo, Arcetri 7 May 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2497); 14–28 May (nos. 2504–2523)

entries.headline: Third deposition and written defence
entries.digest: Given eight days to prepare a defence, Galileo handed in one already written, with Bellarmine's original certificate. He argued that the certificate was what he had relied on for sixteen years. The words 'teach' and 'in any way whatever' had been new to him at the first hearing. The faults of the book came from vainglory, not malice. He asked for mercy for his age, his illnesses and ten months of anxiety.
entries.source_note: Third deposition and defence, 10 May 1633 (Finocchiaro pp. 279–82; Famous Trials, defence)

entries.headline: The Pope decides: examine his intention, then abjure
entries.digest: The minutes record Urban VIII's decision. Galileo was to be questioned about his intention, under the threat of torture. If he sustained his answers, he was to abjure vehement suspicion of heresy before the full Congregation and be imprisoned at its pleasure. He was to be forbidden to treat the Earth's motion again, and the Dialogue was to be prohibited. Copies of the sentence were to go to nuncios and inquisitors, and in Florence it was to be read before professors.
entries.source_note: Holy Office decree ('Sanctissimus'), 16 June 1633 (Finocchiaro; Santillana)

entries.headline: Forty days of prayer against the plague
entries.digest: Four days before the sentence, Maria Celeste wrote that her convent had been ordered to keep forty days of continuous prayer against the plague, two nuns at a time, day and night. She did not yet know what Rome had decided.
entries.source_note: Maria Celeste to Galileo, Arcetri 18 June 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2547)

entries.headline: The Pope forewarns the ambassador
entries.digest: Urban VIII told Niccolini that the sentence would be given within days. He said the opinion of the Earth's motion would be prohibited as erroneous and contrary to Scripture,.
entries.source_note: Niccolini to Cioli, Rome 19 June 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2550)

entries.headline: Fourth deposition, under threat of torture
entries.digest: Asked whether he held or had held that the Sun was the centre and the Earth moved, Galileo said that after the 1616 decree he had held Ptolemy's opinion as true. Told that the book suggested otherwise and that torture could be used, he repeated that he did not hold the Copernican view and was in their hands. The record notes that nothing further could be obtained, and he was returned to his room.
entries.source_note: Fourth deposition, 21 June 1633 (Finocchiaro p. 286); English in Popular Science Monthly 67 (1905)

entries.place: Rome, convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva
entries.headline: Sentence: vehemently suspect of heresy
entries.digest: The sentence recited the case from 1615 and found that Galileo had made himself vehemently suspect of heresy. He had held and believed a doctrine contrary to Scripture, and defended it as probable after it had been declared contrary to Scripture. The Dialogue was prohibited. Galileo was condemned to formal imprisonment at the Holy Office's pleasure and to recite the seven penitential psalms weekly for three years. Of the ten cardinals named, three did not sign: Francesco Barberini, Gaspare Borgia and Laudivio Zacchia.
entries.source_note: Sentence, 22 June 1633 (Finocchiaro pp. 286–91); English in Popular Science Monthly 67 (1905)

entries.headline: The abjuration, on his knees
entries.digest: Kneeling, Galileo read and signed the formula. He abjured the errors and heresies, swore never again to say or write anything that could bring such suspicion on him, and promised to denounce any heretic he knew of. The text was the court's, not his own. No contemporary record has him say anything else; the 'Eppur si muove' story is a later legend.
entries.quote: I abjure, curse, and detest the aforesaid errors and heresies
entries.source_note: Abjuration, 22 June 1633 (Finocchiaro pp. 292–93); English in Popular Science Monthly 67 (1905)

entries.headline: Sentence read, abjuration made, prison commuted
entries.digest: Niccolini told Cioli that Galileo had been called to the Minerva, heard the sentence and abjured. The book was banned and he had been condemned to prison at the Pope's pleasure. But at Tuscany's request the prison had at once been commuted to confinement in the Medici villa at Trinità dei Monti.
entries.source_note: Niccolini to Cioli, Rome 26 June 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2558)

entries.headline: The case as a warning about licences
entries.digest: To the nuncio in Madrid, Cesare Monti, Cardinal Francesco Barberini presented the Galileo case as an example of how errors slipped through careless licensing of books. He noted that the sentence had required Galileo to recant.
entries.source_note: F. Barberini to Monti, Rome, June 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2561; day not given)

entries.headline: Read it to the professors
entries.digest: Cardinal Antonio Barberini, the Pope's brother and a cardinal-inquisitor, sent copies of the sentence and abjuration to the inquisitors, among them the inquisitor of Modena. He ordered that they be read to the professors of philosophy and mathematics, so that all would know the prohibition on teaching Copernicus. The circular turned a sentence on one man into a public notice across Catholic Europe.
entries.source_note: Antonio Barberini to the Inquisitor of Modena, Rome 2 July 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2566)

entries.headline: The news reaches the convent
entries.digest: Maria Celeste wrote that news of the sentence against the book and against his person had given her the deepest grief. She urged him to bear it with the same fortitude he had shown in everything, and to trust in God.
entries.source_note: Maria Celeste to Galileo, Arcetri 2 July 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2563)

entries.headline: Rumours in Provence: enemies and an offended Pope
entries.digest: Peiresc told Pierre Dupuy in Paris the rumours reaching him: that Galileo's enemies had made the affront worse, and that the Pope had taken personal offence. A week later he passed on a report that Galileo had been made to declare publicly that he did not hold the Earth to move.
entries.source_note: Peiresc to Dupuy, Aix 8 and 16 Aug 1633 (Favaro XV nos. 2628, 2644)

entries.headline: Spoiled wine and a storm-damaged house
entries.digest: Maria Celeste was glad her father had signed the petition for his return. She hoped he would come home or at least stay at Siena rather than go to the Certosa. She reported that the wine had spoiled and was being sold, and that a storm had damaged the house. These are the ordinary troubles of a household run from inside a convent for an absent prisoner.
entries.source_note: Maria Celeste to Galileo, Arcetri 13 Aug 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2635)

entries.headline: She has taken on his penance
entries.digest: Maria Celeste told her father that she had taken on his weekly obligation to recite the seven penitential psalms, and had been doing it for some time. The penance imposed on the condemned man was being paid, in fact, by his daughter.
entries.source_note: Maria Celeste to Galileo, Arcetri 3 Oct 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2735)

entries.headline: Descartes decides not to publish
entries.digest: Descartes told Mersenne he had learned that Galileo's Dialogue had been condemned and copies burned at Rome. Since his own Le Monde rested on the Earth's motion, he would not let it appear in a form the Church condemned. He said he had almost resolved to burn his papers. He asked Mersenne what exactly had happened in Rome.
entries.source_note: Descartes to Mersenne, [Deventer, end of November 1633] (Favaro XV no. 2797; Adam & Tannery I); date supplied by editors

entries.headline: Leave to go to the villa, with conditions
entries.digest: Niccolini wrote to Galileo that the Congregation, sitting on Thursday 1 December, had let him move to his villa at Arcetri. He was not to hold gatherings or receive many visitors. Niccolini presented it as a step toward a full pardon. In mid-December Galileo was back at Arcetri, next to his daughters' convent.
entries.source_note: Niccolini to Galileo and to Cioli, Rome 3 Dec 1633 (Favaro XV nos. 2802–2803); Holy Office decree of 1 Dec 1633 (Museo Galileo)

entries.headline: The last surviving letter
entries.digest: Maria Celeste's last surviving letter was written while her father was on the road home. After his return there was no need to write: he was a few minutes' walk from the convent. Her letters end here, four months before her death.
entries.source_note: Maria Celeste to Galileo, Arcetri 10 Dec 1633 (Favaro XV no. 2813)

entries.headline: Condolence, and dismay at new orders
entries.digest: Nine days after Maria Celeste's death, Piccolomini wrote to console Galileo for the loss of his daughter, whose life he called one of rare charity. He added that he was troubled by the new orders from Rome forbidding Galileo to petition again for his freedom.
entries.source_note: Piccolomini to Galileo, Siena 11 April 1634 (Favaro XVI no. 2921)

entries.headline: The hernia, the palpitations, and his daughter
entries.digest: Galileo told Geri Bocchineri that his hernia had returned, his heart raced, and he was sunk in melancholy. He wrote of his constant longing for his dead daughter. He asked that his son Vincenzio not make a journey, and dealt with a payment of 25 scudi. It is the rawest letter of his confinement.
entries.source_note: Galileo to Bocchineri, Arcetri 27 April 1634 (Favaro XVI no. 2927)

entries.headline: Micanzio: a barbarous threat
entries.digest: From Venice, Micanzio called it barbarous that asking for mercy should be treated as an offence. He urged Galileo not to hide his studies but to keep working and publish, which would frustrate his enemies more than anything. Two weeks later he advised prudence after the reply to Galileo's petition.
entries.source_note: Micanzio to Galileo, Venice 29 April and 13 May 1634 (Favaro XVI nos. 2929, 2939)

entries.headline: To Diodati: the whole story, and the Jesuits
entries.digest: Galileo gave Diodati a full account: the sentence, Siena, Arcetri, the pardon that never came. He described his daughter's six-day illness and death. He told of the Inquisitor's vicar warning him that any further plea would bring him back to a Roman prison. He blamed his ruin less on his opinions than on Jesuit hostility, citing a remark attributed to Christoph Grienberger. He listed the books being written against him and said he planned to answer them.
entries.source_note: Galileo to Diodati, Arcetri 25 July 1634 (Favaro XVI no. 2970; Lettere XXIII); English in Gebler (1879), pp. 276–77, dated there 24 July

entries.headline: Peiresc pleads with the Cardinal
entries.digest: Peiresc wrote to Cardinal Francesco Barberini asking mercy for an old, sick man kept at his villa, barred from Florence and from friends. He had lost his one consolation, a daughter who was a nun. He warned that such harshness would be held against the pontificate by posterity,. Barberini replied on 2 January 1635 only that he would put the matter before the Pope; Galileo remained confined at Arcetri until his death on 8 January 1642.
entries.source_note: Peiresc to F. Barberini, Aix 5 Dec 1634 (Favaro XVI no. 3026); reply F. Barberini to Peiresc, Rome 2 Jan 1635 (no. 3050)

entries.headline: Epilogue: the judges erred
entries.digest: Addressing the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, John Paul II received the report of the commission he had set up after his speech of November 1979. He said that most of Galileo's theologians had failed to distinguish Scripture from its interpretation, and so had carried a question of science into the realm of faith. He did not formally annul the sentence. Newspapers around the world nonetheless reported the address as the Church's rehabilitation of Galileo, 359 years after the abjuration.
entries.source_note: Address of 31 Oct 1992 (vatican.va); Christian History Institute, 'Upon Further Review'

claims.claim: Galileo ordered by the Commissary not to hold, teach or defend Copernicanism in any way (unsigned minute)
claims.evidence: Holy Office file, 'Special Injunction' minute; Finocchiaro pp. 147–48

claims.claim: Galileo has not abjured; he was only told the doctrine may not be held or defended
Galileo has meddled in the gravest matters and obtained his licence by deception
claims.evidence: Niccolini's dispatch of 5 Sept 1632 (Favaro XIV no. 2298)

claims.claim: Galileo summoned to appear in Rome during October
Three Florentine physicians certify him unfit to travel; Rome rejects it on 30 December
claims.evidence: Physicians' certificate; Holy Office decree of 30 Dec 1632

claims.claim: Does not recall being ordered not to teach 'in any way'; the book does not defend Copernicus
Consultors Oreggi, Inchofer and Pasqualigo: the Dialogue teaches and defends the Earth's motion
Out of court, Galileo has agreed to confess that he went too far
claims.evidence: Maculano to F. Barberini; Finocchiaro pp. 276–77

claims.claim: Confesses the book overstated Copernican arguments out of vainglory, not intent
Defence: relied on Bellarmine's certificate; 'teach' and 'in any way' were new to him
Pope orders examination on intention under threat of torture, abjuration, imprisonment, ban of the book
Has held Ptolemy's view as true since 1616; 'I am here to obey'
Galileo vehemently suspect of heresy; Dialogue prohibited; formal imprisonment and penance
claims.evidence: Sentence; signed by seven of ten cardinals

claims.claim: Abjures, curses and detests the said errors; 'Eppur si muove' is a later legend (first printed 1757)
claims.evidence: Abjuration; Finocchiaro pp. 292–93; Baretti, Italian Library (1757)

claims.claim: Prison commuted at once to confinement in the Medici villa at Trinità dei Monti
Galileo's theologians erred in treating a scientific question as one of faith; no formal annulment
claims.evidence: Address to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences (vatican.va)

convergences.label: The Pope's anger, written up in the embassy
convergences.note: The only record of the outburst is the ambassador's: the Pope's words are vivid and personal, while Niccolini's covering advice the next day is cool tactics — work through the nephew, make no protest.

convergences.label: Referral to the Holy Office and the summons (18–25 September 1632)
convergences.note: In one week the case moves from a papal audience to a Congregation decree to the nephew's letter to Florence: the same decision seen as private warning, legal order and diplomatic instruction.

convergences.label: The medical certificate fails
convergences.note: In Rome Niccolini reports that the doctors' certificate is being read as a ruse; in Florence, on the same day, Galileo writes to Diodati as if the argument over Scripture and nature were still open.

convergences.label: First hearing and detention (12–20 April 1633)
convergences.note: Galileo writes of his comfortable rooms. The ambassador cannot learn when he will be freed. The consultors quietly find against his defence. In Arcetri his daughter hears only that he is shut in, and in Siena the archbishop hopes for a just end.

convergences.label: The plea arrangement (27 April – 1 May 1633)
convergences.note: Maculano's letter shows the plea arranged from the court's side. Galileo's deposition of the 30th is the confession it produced, and Niccolini credits the Commissary for the early release. Maria Celeste, the same day, is simply glad the case is moving.

convergences.label: Decision, examination and sentence (16–22 June 1633)
convergences.note: The papal decree fixes the outcome before the last examination. The Pope forewarns the ambassador and Galileo answers under threat of torture. Meanwhile his daughter's convent begins forty days of prayer against the plague, unaware.

convergences.label: The sentence goes out (26 June – 2 July 1633)
convergences.note: Niccolini reports the commutation and the Holy Office circulates the sentence to inquisitors for reading to professors. Cardinal Barberini uses it as a lesson on licensing, and in Arcetri the news arrives as grief.

convergences.label: Release to Arcetri and Descartes' retreat (November–December 1633)
convergences.note: As Niccolini negotiates and then announces Galileo's move to Arcetri, Descartes in Deventer shelves Le Monde on the strength of the news alone. The sentence's effect abroad came before its softening at home was known.

convergences.label: The daughter's death and the new prohibition (April 1634)
convergences.note: Three letters in three weeks: the archbishop's condolence, Galileo's account of his own collapse, and Micanzio's anger from Venice at the order that he must not ask for mercy.

ties.note: Father and elder daughter; her letters of 1633 are the only family record of the trial, and his replies are lost.
Niccolini housed Galileo at Villa Medici for most of his five months in Rome and was his advocate with the Pope.
The ambassador's audiences are the source for almost everything the Pope is known to have said privately about the case.
Maculano examined him in all four depositions and talked him into the plea out of court on 27 April 1633.
The Commissary's 28 April letter to the cardinal-nephew is the inside account of how the plea was arranged.
Bellarmine's signed certificate and the unsigned injunction minute of the same 1616 meeting do not agree. The 1633 case turned on that gap.
They met on 26 February 1616; Galileo kept Bellarmine's certificate for seventeen years and produced it at his third hearing.
Once friends: as cardinal, Maffeo Barberini wrote verses praising Galileo and in 1624 received him six times. As Pope he judged that Galileo had deceived him.
Castelli was Galileo's pupil; Galileo's 1613 letter to him on Scripture began the Roman file in 1615.
Maria Celeste wrote of the archbishop's kindness and gifts while her father lived in his palace, and he wrote to console Galileo on her death.
Long-standing correspondents; Peiresc's plea of 5 December 1634 drew only a promise to raise it with the Pope.
Descartes never met Galileo and had not yet seen the Dialogue when he heard of its condemnation, but suppressed his own Copernican Le Monde as a result.
Micanzio's letters from Venice urged Galileo to keep writing, and he later tried, without success, to have the Two New Sciences printed in Venice.
In 1992 a pope judged the 1633 tribunal's theologians to have erred, without formally reversing its sentence.

threads_out.note: The Dialogue's case for Copernicus rested on what the telescope had shown in 1609–1611: Jupiter's moons, the phases of Venus, sunspots. Bellarmine, who delivered the 1616 warning, had asked the Jesuit astronomers of the Roman College in April 1611 to confirm those observations, and they did.

On 8 March 1632, as the Dialogue appeared, Cardinal Gaspare Borgia protested in consistory against Urban VIII's reluctance to back the Habsburg cause in the Thirty Years' War. Many historians link the Pope's need to look firm in defence of the faith with the severity of 1633. Borgia was one of the three cardinals whose names are missing from the sentence.

The Roman Inquisition that tried Galileo was set up by Paul III in 1542 as part of the Catholic response to the Reformation that Luther's refusal to recant at Worms had opened. The procedure of a demanded recantation of one's books runs from one hearing to the other.

Both cases were later revisited by the authority that had condemned the accused: the French courts annulled Dreyfus's conviction in 1906, and the Holy See re-examined Galileo's case from 1979 to 1992. The Galileo review stopped short of an annulment.

images.title: Galileo before the Holy Office
images.caption: Joseph-Nicolas Robert-Fleury's history painting imagines the 1633 hearing. It is a nineteenth-century Romantic reconstruction, not a record: the Holy Office kept no visual record of its sessions.
images.credit: Joseph-Nicolas Robert-Fleury; Musée du Louvre, Paris (via Museo Galileo)

images.title: Galileo before the Tribunal of the Inquisition
images.caption: Niccolò Barabino's reduced replica of his fresco for Palazzo Celesia in Genoa, showing how the trial became a set piece of Risorgimento-era painting.
images.credit: Niccolò Barabino; private collection, Genoa (via Museo Galileo)

images.title: Galileo in prison (attributed to Murillo)
images.caption: A painting of Galileo in a cell, catalogued under Murillo's name. It is the picture often said to carry a hidden 'E pur si muove' inscription; its attribution and date are uncertain, and in 1633 Galileo was held in officials' apartments, not a cell.
images.credit: attributed to Bartolomé Esteban Murillo; location unknown (via Museo Galileo)

images.title: An elderly prisoner, probably Galileo
images.caption: A watercolour by François-Marius Granet, another nineteenth-century image of the confined scientist.
images.credit: François-Marius Granet; Musée des Beaux-Arts, Rennes (via Museo Galileo)

images.title: Frontispiece of the Index of Prohibited Books, 1664
images.caption: The Roman Index issued under Alexander VII, which still listed Galileo's Dialogue among banned books, with Copernicus's book admitted only in corrected form. The Dialogue left the Index only in the edition of 1835.

vantage_key: 0 = the accused and the court (Galileo, the Holy Office file, the Commissary, the Pope); 1 = those in the audience rooms of Rome (the ambassador, the cardinal-nephew, Bellarmine in 1616); 2 = friends in Rome at one remove; 3 = Tuscany and Venice, by letter; 4 = abroad, or long afterwards.
